---
title: "Insight from Psychedelic Research"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-01-31"
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

Diverse PETs exhibit distinct clinical profiles and temporal dynamics. If their mechanisms of action were merely duplicative, their combination would be redundant and offer little added benefit. Yet, clinical practice frequently employs and finds value in combination treatments, such as maintenance pharmacotherapy following ECT, psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy, or the concurrent use of rTMS with medication.

This suggests that while these treatments operate under shared principles, they may have distinct roles in the treatment process. Currently, the field lacks a unifying framework to guide their integration, often relying on sequential or trial-and-error approaches. Developing rational combination strategies that account for individual patient's symptom characteristics and treatment history requires a clearer mapping of where each intervention is uniquely positioned along the axis of treatment process.

In this context, psychedelic research provides a valuable insight. Substances like psilocybin, Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and Dimethyltryptamine (DMT) transiently disrupt canonical functional networks and facilitate global re-integration [@Tagliazucchi2018]. This phenomenon has been dubbed as an "entropic brain state," where the brain transitions into a more flexible regime near "criticality" [@CarhartHarris2014; @CarhartHarris2019]. It is considered therapeutic, however, as it enables the brain to escape from pathological "stuck loops." Recent fMRI studies have confirmed that this acute desynchronization allows the system to access a broader repertoire of potential brain states [@Siegel2024].

Another important insight is that these substances can reopen critical periods for neuroplastic learning [@Hensch2004; @Patton2019]. A critical period is an early developmental window during which the nervous system is exceptionally sensitive to environmental stimuli. Animal studies have demonstrated that the administration of psychedelics to adult mice can re-engage critical periods, particularly in the context of social reward learning [@Nardou2023]. Re-entering a critical period signifies a substantial elevation in neuroplastic potential, facilitating rapid and sustained modifications in structural and functional connectivity. Reflecting this capacity, psychedelics are often termed "psychoplastogens" [@Vargas2021].

Clinicians practicing psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy view this period as a "window of opportunity" for therapeutic change, emphasizing that structured psychotherapeutic interventions must be provided during this time [@CarhartHarris2018; @Lepow2021; @Lepow2023; @Caulfield2025]. This clinical expertise underscores that the critical period reopened by psychedelics serves as a prime opportunity for fundamental change in any direction.

These features of psychedelics map naturally onto an attractor model of psychopathology. Acute $5\text{-HT}_{2\text{A}}$-mediated perturbation transiently reduces within- and between-network integrity, leading to a temporary “flattening” of the attractor landscape and enhanced transitions among metastable states [@Roseman2014; @Madsen2021; @Singleton2022]. Following this disruption, a time-limited window of heightened neuroplasticity opens, during which activity-dependent synaptic remodeling is facilitated via BDNF–TrkB-linked pathways. Clinically, the benefit of psychedelics appears to be time-limited; without structured psychotherapy, clinical gains may attenuate as the system relaxes back toward pre-existing maladaptive attractors [@CarhartHarris2018a; @Goodwin2022]. The existence of a time constraint implies that this malleable state cannot persist indefinitely; the landscape will eventually remodel with distinct valleys and ridges. Consequently, therapeutic remodeling must be actively pursued during this window to reinforce the dynamic resilience of healthy basins and prevent the system from returning to pathological states.
